## Introduction

Picture this: a fellow MSBA student asks you to rate each of your 10 core classes on a scale of 1 to 10. You want to be honest, but you also don't want to seem ungrateful or lazy. So everything gets an 8 or 9. The result? A pile of nearly identical numbers that tells absolutely nothing about what you actually prefer.

This is a real problem in survey research, and smart people have come up with a clever solution: **MaxDiff**, also called Best-Worst Scaling.

Instead of rating each class in isolation, MaxDiff puts you in a series of small competitions. On each screen you see four classes and answer two questions: "Which of these would you most want to take?" and "Which would you least want?" You do this eight times, each time with a different combination of four classes. Because you're making real trade-offs under scarcity rather than assigning abstract numbers, the resulting data is much richer and more honest.

> Think of it like a mini tournament. Every time a class wins (gets picked as best) or loses (gets picked as worst), it earns or loses points. By the end, the rankings emerge naturally from the competition results.

We ran exactly this survey with our MSBA cohort across all 10 core classes. Now we have real choice data, and we're going to analyze it three different ways, each a bit more sophisticated than the last:

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
**What this post covers -- three lenses on the same question**

| Step | Method | What it tells you | Effort |
|------|--------|-------------------|--------|
| **1** | Counts Analysis | Quick scoreboard: % chosen best minus % chosen worst | Low |
| **2** | MNL via Max Likelihood | Precise utility estimates that account for who was on screen | Medium |
| **3** | Bayesian MNL via MCMC | Full probability distributions over preferences + honest uncertainty | High |

All three methods should tell a similar story at the top and bottom of the ranking. Where they differ is in the middle and in how confidently they speak.
:::

By the end you will know which MSBA classes our cohort genuinely wants to take -- and you will understand three powerful statistical tools for measuring preferences.

Here is exactly what one survey screen looked like for each respondent:

```{python}
labels_raw.columns = ["item_num", "full_label"]

    1:  "AI Math & Prog",
    2:  "SQL",
    3:  "Mktg/Fin/Ops",
    4:  "Large Data",
    5:  "Business Analytics",
    6:  "Consulting",
    7:  "Customer Analytics",
    8:  "Capstone",
    9:  "Marketing Analytics",
    10: "Biz Intelligence",
}
labels_raw["short_label"] = labels_raw["item_num"].map(short_labels)
```

The survey design includes two kinds of tasks. Tasks 1-8 are the core MaxDiff screens: each shows four classes and asks for a best and worst pick. Tasks 9-15 are anchor comparison tasks that pair one class against a fixed reference item (item 11), collecting only a best pick. For everything below we use only the main MaxDiff tasks.

```{python}
#| label: filter-tasks
# Keep only tasks that show exactly 4 items (main MaxDiff tasks)
task_sizes = df_raw.groupby(["respondent", "task"]).size()
four_item_tasks = task_sizes[task_sizes == 4].reset_index()[["respondent", "task"]]
df_main = df_raw.merge(four_item_tasks, on=["respondent", "task"])

N      = df_main["respondent"].nunique()
n_tasks_per = df_main.groupby("respondent")["task"].nunique().value_counts().index[0]
J      = 4   # items per task
n_items = 10  # total items
```

The study involved **`{python} N`** respondents, each seeing **`{python} n_tasks_per`** tasks with **4 classes** per task. Across the full design, 10 distinct classes appeared.

**Sanity check:** every task should produce exactly one best pick (response = 1), one worst pick (response = -1), and two neutral picks (response = 0).

```{python}
#| label: sanity-check
g = df_main.groupby(["respondent", "task"])["response"]
sanity = pd.DataFrame({
    "n_best":  g.apply(lambda x: (x == 1).sum()),
    "n_worst": g.apply(lambda x: (x == -1).sum()),
    "n_zero":  g.apply(lambda x: (x == 0).sum()),
}).reset_index()

all_valid = (
    (sanity["n_best"] == 1).all() and
    (sanity["n_worst"] == 1).all() and
    (sanity["n_zero"] == 2).all()
)

status = "PASSED" if all_valid else "FAILED"
print(f"Sanity check {status}: {len(sanity)} tasks checked.")
print(f"Every task has exactly 1 best, 1 worst, and 2 zero responses: {all_valid}")
```

**Exposure balance:** a well-designed MaxDiff study shows each item roughly the same number of times so no class has an unfair data advantage.

```{python}

styled_table(exposure)
```

## Counts Analysis

Let's start simple. The counts score for each class answers one question: when a class showed up, did students want it or avoid it?

$$\text{score}_j = \frac{\text{times chosen as best}}{\text{times shown}} - \frac{\text{times chosen as worst}}{\text{times shown}}$$

Reading the score is easy:
- **Score close to +1:** Students almost always picked this class as their favorite when it appeared. A crowd favorite.
- **Score close to -1:** Students almost always ranked this class last. Tough crowd.
- **Score close to 0:** The class is middle of the pack, or students are split on it.

The counts approach is fast, honest, and needs zero modeling assumptions. You can explain it to anyone in under a minute. Its one weakness: it doesn't account for *who else was on screen*. A class that kept getting shown against the two most popular classes will look worse than it really is. That's exactly what the MNL model fixes. But for now, let's see what the raw data tells us.

```{python}
#| label: counts
counts = (df_main.groupby("item")
                 .agg(shown=("response", "count"),
                      n_best=("response", lambda x: (x == 1).sum()),
                      n_worst=("response", lambda x: (x == -1).sum()))
                 .reset_index())
counts["pct_best"]  = counts["n_best"]  / counts["shown"]
counts["pct_worst"] = counts["n_worst"] / counts["shown"]
counts["score"]     = counts["pct_best"] - counts["pct_worst"]
counts = (counts.merge(labels_raw[["item_num","short_label"]],
                        left_on="item", right_on="item_num")
                .sort_values("score", ascending=False)
                .reset_index(drop=True))
counts["rank"] = counts.index + 1
```

```{python}
#| label: bootstrap
#| cache: true
np.random.seed(42)
B       = 1000
resp_list = df_main["respondent"].unique()
N_resp  = len(resp_list)

# Pre-split by respondent for speed
resp_dict = {r: df_main[df_main["respondent"] == r] for r in resp_list}

boot_mat = np.zeros((10, B))
for b in range(B):
    samp = np.random.choice(resp_list, N_resp, replace=True)
    boot_df = pd.concat([resp_dict[r] for r in samp], ignore_index=True)
    for j in range(1, 11):
        sub = boot_df[boot_df["item"] == j]
        shown = len(sub)
        if shown > 0:
            boot_mat[j-1, b] = ((sub["response"] == 1).sum() -
                                  (sub["response"] == -1).sum()) / shown

ci_low  = np.percentile(boot_mat, 2.5,  axis=1)  # shape (10,)
ci_high = np.percentile(boot_mat, 97.5, axis=1)

counts["ci_low"]  = counts["item"].map(dict(zip(range(1,11), ci_low)))
counts["ci_high"] = counts["item"].map(dict(zip(range(1,11), ci_high)))
```

## From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices

The counts score is a great starting point, but it's missing something important. Imagine a class that keeps getting shown alongside the two most popular classes in the survey. It's always going to look bad by comparison, even if it would crush a different set of competitors. The counts approach can't tell the difference.

The **multinomial logit (MNL) model** can. It models the actual probability of each pick, given exactly who was on screen at the time.

The MNL assigns each class $j$ a utility $\beta_j$. When a task shows items $\{a, b, c, d\}$, the probability that item $b$ is picked as best uses the softmax formula:

$$P(\text{best} = b) = \frac{\exp(\beta_b)}{\exp(\beta_a) + \exp(\beta_b) + \exp(\beta_c) + \exp(\beta_d)}$$

After the best is removed, the worst is picked from the remaining three using negated utilities (because the worst pick goes to the least preferred item):

$$P(\text{worst} = c \mid \text{best} = b) = \frac{\exp(-\beta_c)}{\exp(-\beta_a) + \exp(-\beta_c) + \exp(-\beta_d)}$$

So each 4-item task yields **two** observations: one MNL choice from the full set (best) and one from the reduced set of 3 (worst).

**A note on identifiability:** the softmax is unchanged if you add any constant to all betas. We cannot estimate unique values for all 10 betas without a normalization. The convention here is to fix $\beta_1 = 0$ and estimate the remaining nine betas relative to class 1 (AI Math and Prog). Positive estimates mean "more preferred than AI Math," negative means "less preferred."

The chart below shows how the softmax formula translates utility values into pick probabilities. Try to build the intuition: a class with utility 2 is not twice as likely to be picked as a class with utility 1. The relationship is exponential.

```{python}
#| label: softmax-explainer
#| echo: false
import itertools
beta_demo = np.array([-1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0])
labels_demo = ["Class A\n(β = -1)", "Class B\n(β = 0)", "Class C\n(β = 1)", "Class D\n(β = 2)"]
probs_demo = np.exp(beta_demo) / np.exp(beta_demo).sum()
colors_demo = [RED, AMBER, BLUE, GREEN]

fig_sm = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2,
    subplot_titles=["Utility values (β)", "Choice probabilities from softmax"],
    horizontal_spacing=0.15)

fig_sm.add_trace(go.Bar(
    x=labels_demo, y=beta_demo, marker_color=colors_demo, showlegend=False,
    text=[f"β = {v:.0f}" for v in beta_demo], textposition="outside",
    hovertemplate="<b>%{x}</b><br>Utility: %{y}<extra></extra>",
), row=1, col=1)

fig_sm.add_trace(go.Bar(
    x=labels_demo, y=probs_demo, marker_color=colors_demo, showlegend=False,
    text=[f"{p:.1%}" for p in probs_demo], textposition="outside",
    hovertemplate="<b>%{x}</b><br>P(best): %{y:.1%}<extra></extra>",
), row=1, col=2)

fig_sm.update_yaxes(title_text="Utility (β)", row=1, col=1)
fig_sm.update_yaxes(title_text="P(chosen as best)", tickformat=".0%", range=[0, 0.75], row=1, col=2)
fig_sm.update_layout(
    title=dict(text="How utilities become probabilities: the softmax in action",
               font=dict(size=15, color=NAVY)),
    paper_bgcolor=LIGHT, plot_bgcolor=LIGHT,
    bargap=0.3, height=420, margin=dict(l=60, r=40, t=80, b=60),
)
show(fig_sm)
```

Class D has a utility of 2 -- four times higher than Class A's -1 in raw numbers. But through the softmax it wins **`{python} f"{probs_demo[3]:.0%}"`** of choices vs Class A's **`{python} f"{probs_demo[0]:.0%}"`**. The MNL captures this nonlinear relationship precisely, which is something a simple count of wins and losses cannot do.

```{python}
#| label: reshape-tasks
# Build one row per task: which items were shown, which was best, which was worst
task_rows = []
for (resp, task), grp in df_main.groupby(["respondent", "task"]):
    grp_sorted = grp.sort_values("position")
    items = grp_sorted["item"].tolist()
    best  = grp_sorted.loc[grp_sorted["response"] ==  1, "item"].values
    worst = grp_sorted.loc[grp_sorted["response"] == -1, "item"].values
    if len(best) == 1 and len(worst) == 1:
        task_rows.append({
            "respondent": resp, "task": task,
            "items": items,
            "best": int(best[0]), "worst": int(worst[0])
        })

task_df = pd.DataFrame(task_rows)

# Pre-compute arrays for vectorized likelihood
items_mat = np.array(task_df["items"].tolist(), dtype=int)  # (n_tasks, 4)
best_arr  = task_df["best"].values                           # (n_tasks,)
worst_arr = task_df["worst"].values                          # (n_tasks,)

print(f"Tasks ready for MNL: {len(task_df):,} tasks from {N} respondents")
```

---

## MNL via Maximum Likelihood

The log-likelihood sums over every task, collecting the log-probability of both the best and worst picks:

$$\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \sum_{\text{tasks}} \Bigg[ \underbrace{\beta_{j^*_b} - \log \!\!\!\sum_{j \in \text{shown}}\!\!\! \exp(\beta_j)}_{\text{best pick}} - \underbrace{\beta_{j^*_w} + \log \!\!\!\!\!\sum_{j \in \text{shown} \setminus \{j^*_b\}}\!\!\!\!\! \exp(-\beta_j)}_{\text{worst pick}} \Bigg]$$

The code below implements this in a vectorized form. Rather than looping over tasks, we use NumPy array indexing to compute all utilities at once, and `scipy.special.logsumexp` for numerical stability.

```{python}
#| label: ll-function
def ll(beta_free, items_mat, best_arr, worst_arr):
    """
    Log-likelihood of the MaxDiff MNL model.
    beta_free: length-9 array (beta_2 through beta_10; beta_1 = 0 is reference)
    """
    beta = np.concatenate([[0.0], beta_free])  # beta[0] = 0 for item 1

    # Utilities for all shown items (n_tasks x 4)
    # items_mat has values 1-10; convert to 0-indexed
    u = beta[items_mat - 1]                      # shape (n_tasks, 4)

    # Best pick: util(best) - log(sum(exp(utils)))
    u_best       = beta[best_arr - 1]            # shape (n_tasks,)
    log_norm_best = logsumexp(u, axis=1)         # numerically stable
    lp_best      = u_best - log_norm_best

    # Worst pick: -util(worst) - log(sum(exp(-utils)) for remaining 3 items)
    # Trick: sum over all 4, then subtract the best item's contribution
    sum_neg_all    = np.exp(logsumexp(-u, axis=1))
    sum_neg_remain = np.maximum(sum_neg_all - np.exp(-u_best), 1e-300)
    lp_worst       = -beta[worst_arr - 1] - np.log(sum_neg_remain)

    return float(np.sum(lp_best + lp_worst))
```

```{python}
#| label: mle
#| cache: true
def neg_ll(beta_free):
    return -ll(beta_free, items_mat, best_arr, worst_arr)

result = minimize(
    neg_ll,
    x0     = np.zeros(9),
    method = "BFGS",
    options= {"maxiter": 1000, "gtol": 1e-8}
)

beta_mle_free = result.x
beta_mle_full = np.concatenate([[0.0], beta_mle_free])   # full 10-vector

# Standard errors from inverse Hessian (BFGS approximation)
se_free = np.sqrt(np.diag(result.hess_inv))
se_full = np.concatenate([[np.nan], se_free])

# Shares of preference: exp(beta) / sum(exp(beta))
shares_mle = np.exp(beta_mle_full) / np.exp(beta_mle_full).sum()

print(f"Optimizer converged: {result.success}  |  "
      f"Log-likelihood at MLE: {-result.fun:.2f}")
```

When we say "maximum likelihood," it helps to see the actual surface being maximized. Below we hold all betas fixed at their MLE values and scan just one of them -- the beta for Customer Analytics -- across a range. The curve peaks exactly at the MLE estimate, confirming the optimizer found the right answer.

## MNL via Bayesian Estimation

Maximum likelihood gives us a single best guess for each beta, plus a standard error. That's useful, but it's just one number. Bayesian estimation goes further: instead of one answer, it gives us a full **probability distribution** over every possible value of each beta.

Why does that matter? Because we often care about derived quantities like shares of preference. Shares are a nonlinear transformation of the betas, so their uncertainty is tricky to compute from MLE alone (it requires an approximation called the delta method). With Bayesian MCMC, we can just push every sample through the share formula and take percentiles directly. No approximation needed.

The framework is Bayes' rule applied to model parameters:

$$\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \text{data}) \propto L(\boldsymbol{\beta}) \cdot \pi(\boldsymbol{\beta})$$

The posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the prior. We use a weakly informative prior: each free beta gets an independent normal prior centered at 0 with standard deviation $\sqrt{10} \approx 3.16$. This is diffuse enough that the data, not the prior, drives the estimates.

Since we cannot sample from the posterior analytically, we use the **Metropolis-Hastings** algorithm. The idea: start somewhere in parameter space, propose a random step, accept or reject based on the ratio of posterior densities, and repeat thousands of times. The accepted draws trace out the posterior distribution.

```{python}
#| label: mh-sampler
def log_prior(beta_free):
    return np.sum(stats.norm.logpdf(beta_free, loc=0, scale=np.sqrt(10)))

def log_post(beta_free):
    return ll(beta_free, items_mat, best_arr, worst_arr) + log_prior(beta_free)

def mh_sampler(log_post_fn, beta0, n_iter, step, seed=123):
    np.random.seed(seed)
    K       = len(beta0)
    draws   = np.zeros((n_iter, K))
    beta    = beta0.copy()
    lp      = log_post_fn(beta)
    n_accept = 0

    for t in range(n_iter):
        beta_prop = beta + np.random.normal(0, step, K)
        lp_prop   = log_post_fn(beta_prop)

        if np.log(np.random.uniform()) < lp_prop - lp:
            beta     = beta_prop
            lp       = lp_prop
            n_accept += 1

        draws[t] = beta

    return draws, n_accept / n_iter
```

```{python}
#| label: run-mcmc
#| cache: true
n_iter = 20_000
step   = 0.15

draws, accept_rate = mh_sampler(log_post, beta0=beta_mle_free,
                                 n_iter=n_iter, step=step, seed=123)

print(f"Ran {n_iter:,} iterations  |  Step size: {step}")
print(f"Acceptance rate: {accept_rate:.1%}  (target: 25-40%)")
```

The acceptance rate of ~30% (your result may vary slightly) lands comfortably in the target range of 25-40% for a 9-dimensional random walk. This means the chain explores efficiently: not so small that it barely moves, not so large that almost every proposal gets rejected.

### MCMC Diagnostics

Before trusting the posterior, we need to confirm the chain has converged. The telltale sign of a healthy chain is a "fuzzy caterpillar" trace plot: the chain wanders up and down rapidly, with no obvious drift or stuck stretches. Use the slider below to zoom into any section.

```{python}
#| label: trace-plots
burn_in     = n_iter // 4         # discard first 25%
post_draws  = draws[burn_in:]     # post-burn-in draws

# Show traces for 3 interesting parameters (Customer Analytics, Mktg Analytics, SQL)
# These are column indices into the 9-vector of free betas
# beta_free[k] corresponds to item (k+2), so item j -> column (j-2)
param_map = {7: "Customer Analytics", 9: "Marketing Analytics", 2: "SQL"}
trace_colors = [BLUE, GREEN, AMBER]

fig_trace = go.Figure()
for (col_idx, label), color in zip(param_map.items(), trace_colors):
    beta_col = col_idx - 2  # 0-indexed into beta_free
    fig_trace.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x    = list(range(len(post_draws))),
        y    = post_draws[:, beta_col],
        mode = "lines",
        name = label,
        line = dict(color=color, width=0.7),
    ))

fig_trace.update_layout(
    title  = dict(text="MCMC Trace Plots (post burn-in) -- drag the slider to zoom in",
                  font=dict(size=15, color=NAVY)),
    xaxis  = dict(title="Iteration (post burn-in)", rangeslider=dict(visible=True)),
    yaxis  = dict(title="Beta value"),
    legend = dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.05, x=0),
    paper_bgcolor = LIGHT,
    plot_bgcolor  = LIGHT,
    height = 480,
    margin = dict(l=60, r=40, t=80, b=80),
)
show(fig_trace)
```

The chains show rapid mixing with no obvious drift - the "fuzzy caterpillar" pattern we want to see. We discard the first 25% of draws as burn-in and use the remaining `{python} len(post_draws)` draws for inference.

### Posterior Estimates

```{python}
#| label: bayes-results
# Full beta draws: prepend the reference column (beta_1 = 0)
draws_full   = np.hstack([np.zeros((len(post_draws), 1)), post_draws])

# Posterior summaries for each item
beta_post    = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.mean(post_draws, axis=0)])
ci_low_post  = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.percentile(post_draws, 2.5,  axis=0)])
ci_high_post = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.percentile(post_draws, 97.5, axis=0)])

# Posterior shares: compute share for EVERY draw, then take posterior mean
exp_draws       = np.exp(draws_full)                          # (n_draws, 10)
shares_per_draw = exp_draws / exp_draws.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
shares_bayes    = shares_per_draw.mean(axis=0)
shares_low_b    = np.percentile(shares_per_draw, 2.5,  axis=0)
shares_high_b   = np.percentile(shares_per_draw, 97.5, axis=0)

bayes_df = labels_raw[labels_raw["item_num"] <= 10].copy()
bayes_df["beta_post"]   = beta_post
bayes_df["ci_low"]      = ci_low_post
bayes_df["ci_high"]     = ci_high_post
bayes_df["share_bayes"] = shares_bayes
bayes_df["share_low"]   = shares_low_b
bayes_df["share_high"]  = shares_high_b
bayes_df = bayes_df.sort_values("share_bayes", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
bayes_df["rank_bayes"]  = bayes_df.index + 1

display_bayes = bayes_df[["rank_bayes","short_label","beta_post",
                            "ci_low","ci_high","share_bayes",
                            "share_low","share_high"]].copy()
display_bayes["CI (Beta)"]  = display_bayes.apply(
    lambda r: f"[{r['ci_low']:.2f}, {r['ci_high']:.2f}]", axis=1)
display_bayes["CI (Share)"] = display_bayes.apply(
    lambda r: f"[{r['share_low']:.1%}, {r['share_high']:.1%}]", axis=1)
display_bayes["beta_post"]   = display_bayes["beta_post"].map("{:.3f}".format)
display_bayes["share_bayes"] = display_bayes["share_bayes"].map("{:.1%}".format)
display_bayes = display_bayes[["rank_bayes","short_label","beta_post",
                                "CI (Beta)","share_bayes","CI (Share)"]].copy()
display_bayes.columns = ["Rank","Class","Post. Mean Beta","95% CI (Beta)",
                           "Post. Mean Share","95% CI (Share)"]
styled_table(display_bayes)
```

The Bayesian posterior means and the MLE point estimates are very close for every class, as expected when the sample size is moderate and the prior is weakly informative. The posterior standard deviations (half the width of the 95% CI, roughly) should also be close to the MLE standard errors -- and they are. Any small differences come from the prior pulling extreme estimates slightly toward zero, which shrinks the posterior slightly relative to the likelihood-only MLE. The key advantage of the Bayesian approach is not accuracy on the betas themselves, but that the credible intervals on derived quantities like shares are computed by pushing every MCMC draw through the softmax and taking quantiles directly -- no delta-method approximation needed.

One of the most powerful things Bayesian MCMC gives us is a *picture* of uncertainty. The violin plot below shows the full posterior distribution for all 9 free betas (the reference class, AI Math & Prog, is fixed at 0). Each violin is built from 15,000 MCMC draws. The width of the violin at any height tells you how much probability mass is near that beta value -- fat in the middle means that value is likely, thin at the extremes means uncertain.

## Comparing the Three Methods

Now for the fun part: put all three methods side by side and see where they agree, where they disagree, and why.

```{python}
#| label: comparison-table
comp = (counts[["item","short_label","score","rank"]]
              .rename(columns={"score":"score_counts","rank":"rank_counts"})
              .merge(mle_df[["item_num","share","rank"]].rename(
                      columns={"item_num":"item","share":"share_mle","rank":"rank_mle"}),
                     on="item")
              .merge(bayes_df[["item_num","share_bayes","rank_bayes"]].rename(
                      columns={"item_num":"item"}),
                     on="item")
              .sort_values("rank_mle"))

display_comp = comp[["rank_mle","short_label","score_counts","rank_counts",
                      "share_mle","rank_mle","share_bayes","rank_bayes"]].copy()
display_comp["score_counts"] = display_comp["score_counts"].map("{:.3f}".format)
display_comp["share_mle"]    = display_comp["share_mle"].map("{:.1%}".format)
display_comp["share_bayes"]  = display_comp["share_bayes"].map("{:.1%}".format)
display_comp.columns = ["MLE Rank","Class","Counts Score","Counts Rank",
                         "MLE Share","MLE Rank","Bayes Share","Bayes Rank"]
styled_table(display_comp)
```

Before looking at all three methods in the big chart, here is a quick check that MLE and Bayesian agree with each other. If the two approaches are consistent, every dot below should fall close to the diagonal. Points far off the diagonal would signal a real discrepancy worth investigating.


All 10 classes sit very close to the diagonal, confirming that MLE and Bayes tell the same story. The tiny deviations you see are due to the regularizing effect of the prior: the Bayesian estimates are slightly pulled toward zero compared to the MLE.

The scatter shows that MLE and Bayes agree. But do the *rankings* stay stable across all three methods? A **bump chart** is the clearest way to answer that. Each line is one class. Follow a line left-to-right to see how its rank moves from Counts to MLE to Bayesian. Lines that stay flat mean the method doesn't change the verdict. Lines that cross mean the ranking flipped.

```{python}
#| label: bump-chart
#| echo: false
bump_colors = make_gradient(10)[::-1]  # rank 1 = green
bump_color_map = {row["short_label"]: bump_colors[int(row["rank_mle"]) - 1]
                  for _, row in comp.iterrows()}

x_positions  = [0, 1, 2]
x_labels     = ["Counts", "MLE", "Bayesian"]

fig_bump = go.Figure()

for _, row in comp.sort_values("rank_mle").iterrows():
    lbl   = row["short_label"]
    col   = bump_color_map[lbl]
    ranks = [row["rank_counts"], row["rank_mle"], row["rank_bayes"]]

    fig_bump.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=x_positions, y=ranks,
        mode="lines+markers",
        name=lbl,
        line=dict(color=col, width=2.5),
        marker=dict(size=11, color=col, line=dict(color="white", width=1.5)),
        hovertemplate=(f"<b>{lbl}</b><br>"
                       "Method: %{customdata}<br>Rank: %{y}<extra></extra>"),
        customdata=x_labels,
        showlegend=True,
    ))
    # Label at the right end
    fig_bump.add_annotation(
        x=2.06, y=row["rank_bayes"],
        text=f"<b>{lbl}</b>",
        showarrow=False,
        font=dict(size=10, color=col),
        xanchor="left",
    )

fig_bump.update_layout(
    title=dict(text="Rank bump chart -- follow each line across all three methods",
               font=dict(size=15, color=NAVY)),
    xaxis=dict(
        tickvals=x_positions, ticktext=x_labels,
        range=[-0.25, 3.2],
        tickfont=dict(size=13),
        showgrid=False,
    ),
    yaxis=dict(
        autorange="reversed",
        tickvals=list(range(1, 11)),
        title="Rank (1 = most preferred)",
        gridcolor="#e2e8f0",
    ),
    paper_bgcolor=LIGHT, plot_bgcolor=LIGHT,
    legend=dict(orientation="v", x=1.18, y=0.5, xanchor="left",
                font=dict(size=10)),
    height=560, margin=dict(l=60, r=200, t=70, b=60),
)
show(fig_bump)
```

The top and bottom of the ranking are almost perfectly stable -- the lines for Customer Analytics and Marketing Analytics are flat at the top, while Capstone and Biz Intelligence are flat at the bottom. The middle of the chart is where the action is: several classes trade places between methods. Those crossing lines are exactly where MNL adds information over the counts score and where Bayesian credible intervals reveal genuine uncertainty.

```{python}
#| label: comparison-plot
# Color each item consistently across panels (by MLE rank, green=top, red=bottom)
mle_sorted_for_color = mle_df.sort_values("rank")
colors_n = make_gradient(10)
item_color_map = {row["short_label"]: colors_n[row["rank"] - 1]
                  for _, row in mle_sorted_for_color.iterrows()}

def make_method_bar(df_sorted, x_col, hover_label, fmt=".3f"):
    bar_colors = [item_color_map.get(lbl, BLUE) for lbl in df_sorted["short_label"]]
    return go.Bar(
        x             = df_sorted[x_col],
        y             = df_sorted["short_label"],
        orientation   = "h",
        marker_color  = bar_colors,
        text          = df_sorted[x_col].map(("{:" + fmt + "}").format),
        textposition  = "outside",
        showlegend    = False,
        hovertemplate = f"<b>%{{y}}</b><br>{hover_label}: %{{x:{fmt}}}<extra></extra>",
    )

counts_sorted = counts.sort_values("score", ascending=True)
mle_s         = mle_df.sort_values("share", ascending=True)
bayes_s       = bayes_df.sort_values("share_bayes", ascending=True)

fig_comp = make_subplots(
    rows=3, cols=1,
    subplot_titles=[
        "Method 1: Counts Score (% best minus % worst)",
        "Method 2: MLE Share of Preference",
        "Method 3: Bayesian Posterior Mean Share",
    ],
    vertical_spacing=0.09,
)
fig_comp.add_trace(make_method_bar(counts_sorted, "score",       "Score"),       row=1, col=1)
fig_comp.add_trace(make_method_bar(mle_s,         "share",       "Share", ".1%"), row=2, col=1)
fig_comp.add_trace(make_method_bar(bayes_s,       "share_bayes", "Share", ".1%"), row=3, col=1)

fig_comp.update_xaxes(tickformat=".2f", row=1, col=1)
fig_comp.update_xaxes(tickformat=".0%", row=2, col=1)
fig_comp.update_xaxes(tickformat=".0%", row=3, col=1)
fig_comp.update_yaxes(automargin=True, tickfont=dict(size=12))
fig_comp.update_layout(
    title      = dict(text="All Three Methods -- Same Data, Three Lenses",
                      font=dict(size=17, color=NAVY)),
    paper_bgcolor = LIGHT,
    plot_bgcolor  = LIGHT,
    bargap     = 0.30,
    height     = 1500,
    margin     = dict(l=10, r=110, t=80, b=50),
)
show(fig_comp)
```

**Where all three methods agree:** the top and bottom of the ranking are rock solid. Customer Analytics and Marketing Analytics sit at the top in every method. Capstone and Business Intelligence sit at the bottom in every method. When three completely different approaches all point to the same answer, you can be confident in the result.

**Where they disagree:** the middle. Classes like SQL, Mktg/Fin/Ops, and Large Data are tightly clustered with very similar scores. A small amount of noise in the counts approach can flip their order from run to run. The MNL model extracts more information from the same data because every class that appears on screen and *does not* get chosen contributes to the likelihood. That additional signal helps separate the middle-tier classes more cleanly.

**What the MNL adds over counts:** the MNL knows who was on screen during every pick. A class that kept getting shown alongside the two favorites has a hard life in the counts analysis. The MNL adjusts for this automatically, which is why its rankings can diverge from the counts in the middle.

**What Bayes adds over MLE:** honest uncertainty on every number we care about. The credible intervals on shares are computed by pushing 15,000 posterior draws through the softmax formula and taking the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. No approximation, no delta method. With MLE you only get a point estimate plus a standard error on the beta; the uncertainty on the share itself requires extra work. Bayes gives it to you for free.

---

## Discussion

### What did we find?

The answer is surprisingly clear: MSBA students want the career-focused, applied analytics courses. Customer Analytics and Marketing Analytics sit at the top of every ranking by a comfortable margin. These are the classes where you learn techniques you can use in a job interview or on day one of a new role.

The Capstone landing near the bottom is interesting. It is arguably the most valuable experience in the program in hindsight, but the preference data suggests that students anticipate it with more anxiety than excitement. An open-ended project with an external client is intimidating before it starts. Business Intelligence systems similarly ranks low, perhaps because it is perceived as more technical-infrastructure than analytics-application.

### Pick the right tool for the job

All three methods told the same big story. But they have different strengths depending on what you need:

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
**Method Cheat Sheet**

| If you need... | Use... |
|----------------|--------|
| A quick summary you can explain in 30 seconds | **Counts analysis** |
| A rigorous point estimate with classical standard errors | **MLE MNL** |
| Honest uncertainty on derived quantities like market shares | **Bayesian MNL** |
| Individual-level preference estimates (future work) | **Hierarchical Bayes** |
:::

### Caveats

This survey was conducted on one cohort of self-selected MSBA students. Preferences almost certainly shift as students progress through the program -- a first-year student who has not yet taken Capstone will rank it differently than someone who just finished it. Item presentation order can also influence responses: a class that appears early in the survey may be evaluated differently than one that shows up repeatedly at the end. Prior coursework outside the MSBA, current program standing, and career concentration all likely shape preferences in ways our model cannot separate. These results are a snapshot of one group at one point in time, and should not be treated as universal truths about MSBA preferences.

### What comes next?

The most exciting extension is the **hierarchical (mixed) logit** model. Instead of one set of betas for the whole cohort, we would estimate a distribution over student-level betas. That model could answer questions like: "Do students with engineering backgrounds prefer methods courses while business students prefer application courses?" or "Is there a cluster of students who consistently disagree with the majority?" The Bayesian MCMC framework we built here is the natural foundation for that richer analysis.
